strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely novel and practically motivated inverse problem: reconstructing floorplans from human-walked trajectories, where the forward operator (path planning) is non-linear, non-differentiable, and partially observable — a setting largely unexplored in the diffusion-based inverse solver literature.

The core idea is elegant: side-stepping the unstable Jacobian of differentiable path planners by reformulating the likelihood score in a learned contrastive embedding space, with a derivation (Appendix A) connecting InfoNCE-optimal encoders to likelihood ratios following Oord et al. (2018).

Comprehensive experimental design: 6 diverse baselines (DPS with three differentiable planners, DiffPIR, DMPlug, CFG), three trajectory-density regimes, ablations for the intersection penalty, optimizer choice (Adam vs. GD under DDPM/DDIM), measurement noise robustness, and uncertainty quantification via distance-transform variance.

Thorough appendix with implementation details, planner analyses, additional qualitative results, and retrieval analysis in the contrastive space; a reproducibility statement with promised open-source code and public datasets.
Analysis of why differentiable-planner-based guidance fails (Fig. 1 sensitivity study, Jacobian magnitude argument) is convincing and well motivated.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim — that the contrastive similarity gradient is a 'valid approximation' of the true likelihood score — is overstated. The InfoNCE–likelihood equivalence holds only at the exact optimum with infinite negatives and an optimal score function; finite-batch supervised multi-positive training gives no guarantee that ∇x⟨fφ(x),gψ(y)⟩ matches ∇x log p(y|x). No bound, calibration experiment, or empirical verification of surrogate fidelity to the true likelihood is provided.

Evaluation is entirely synthetic and arguably circular: trajectories are generated by A* on HouseExpo floorplans, the contrastive encoders are trained on A*-generated trajectories, and the ground truth against which methods are evaluated is the same A* operator. The motivating application (human walking, IMU sensors) is never tested with real human trajectory data, so claims of practical applicability are unsupported.

The CFG baseline beats CoGuide in the dense regime (0.97 F1 vs 0.95, 0.95 IoU vs 0.90) and is competitive elsewhere; the claim that CFG 'overfits' rests on anecdotal qualitative evidence rather than a quantitative failure mode. The contribution is thus mainly in the sparse/moderate regimes.

Several DPS+X and DMPlug baseline results look suspiciously poor (DMPlug F1 ≈ 0.28–0.31, far below even a trivial prior sampler; DPS variants degrade as trajectories get denser), raising concerns about under-tuned or misconfigured baselines.

Notational and formula errors undermine confidence: in Eqs. 9 and 10 the numerator and denominator of the contrastive losses are identical as written; Appendix C.3 applies fφ to trajectories and gψ to floorplans inconsistently with Section 3.2, and the loss expressions contain apparent errors; the derived noise model (additive Gaussian on trajectories) contradicts the discrete nature of A* paths.

Engineering components (Adam inside DDIM steps, cosine LR annealing with hard gating, intersection penalty) are heuristic and only weakly connected to the theoretical framing; the intersection penalty is a hand-crafted term that partially duplicates the role of the learned guidance.

Generalization claims (city maps from GPS, molecular structure, network topologies) are speculative; only one dataset at 64×64 resolution is evaluated, so the breadth of the claimed 'spatial inverse problems' contribution is unverified.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely interesting and relatively unexplored inverse problem (floorplan reconstruction from walking trajectories) with a non-differentiable, non-invertible forward operator, which is a meaningful addition to the literature on diffusion-based inverse solvers.

The core idea of replacing the unstable path-planner likelihood score with a contrastively learned embedding-space surrogate is intuitive and well-motivated; the InfoNCE/likelihood-ratio connection provides a reasonable conceptual justification (Appendix A derivation).

The evaluation includes six baselines spanning differentiable-planner variants of DPS, plug-and-play solvers (DiffPIR, DMPlug), and CFG, plus ablations on the intersection penalty, optimizer choice (Adam vs GD), and measurement noise, along with a useful uncertainty quantification analysis.
Strong results in the sparse and moderate trajectory-density regimes where the problem is most ill-posed, with a graceful degradation analysis under sensor noise.
Reproducibility statement and detailed implementation hyperparameters in the appendix are commendable.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to a single synthetic dataset (HouseExpo) at 64x64 resolution with trajectories generated by A* — the same operator family used to train the contrastive embedding. There is no real human-walked trajectory data, so the central claim that the method handles the actual 'human walking policy' forward operator is unsupported; the model may simply learn to invert A*, the very operator the paper claims to side-step.

The CFG baseline substantially outperforms CoGuide in the dense regime (0.97 vs 0.95 F1, 0.95 vs 0.90 IoU) and is competitive elsewhere. Since CFG also learns the coupling between trajectories and floorplans implicitly, the paper does not clearly establish what advantage the contrastive surrogate offers over simply training a conditional model, beyond the sparse-regime gain.

Theoretical claims are informal: the InfoNCE-as-likelihood argument holds only at the exact optimum of the contrastive objective with correct density modeling, and no evidence is given that the learned encoders approach this optimum (e.g., mutual information estimates or calibration of the surrogate likelihood). The claimed Lipschitz smoothness of the embedding space is asserted, not demonstrated or measured.

The DPS+NeuralA* baseline reports essentially identical numbers across all three trajectory densities (0.79/0.67 in sparse, moderate, and dense), which is surprising and calls for explanation; the reliability of some baseline configurations is questionable.

The two evaluation metrics (IoU and F1 over free-space pixels) are near-duplicates; additional metrics (e.g., wall topology accuracy, room-count correctness, perceptual/structural similarity) would strengthen the evidence.

Several engineering components (intersection penalty, Adam-in-DDIM with cosine annealing, hard-gating) are presented as necessary for good results but are justified only empirically; the contribution risks reading as a collection of tricks rather than a principled method.

The method requires a matched corpus of (floorplan, trajectory) pairs for training the contrastive encoders, which somewhat undercuts the claimed generality to blind inverse problems and broader operator families — these generalization claims are left entirely to future work.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem setting: reformulating floorplan reconstruction from trajectories as a spatial inverse problem with a non-differentiable, non-invertible forward operator (path planning) is a fresh and practically relevant direction for diffusion-based inverse solvers.

The core idea is clean and well-executed: replacing the unstable likelihood score ∇x‖y−A(x)‖² with a smooth contrastive embedding-space surrogate, with a plausible theoretical justification via the InfoNCE–density-ratio connection (Appendix A) and a sensible extension to multi-positive supervised contrastive training.

Thorough empirical evaluation: six diverse baselines (DPS+three differentiable planners, DiffPIR, DMPlug, CFG), three trajectory-density regimes to probe ill-posedness, measurement-noise robustness, ablations (intersection penalty, Adam vs. GD under DDPM/DDIM), uncertainty quantification via distance-transform variance, and embedding-space analysis (t-SNE, top-5 retrieval).
Good engineering contributions for practical guidance: intersection penalty for wall–trajectory compatibility and Adam-in-DDIM guidance with cosine annealing, both supported by ablations.
Strong reproducibility posture: public dataset, detailed architecture and hyperparameter descriptions (Appendix C), planner implementations and checkpoints documented, and a code release promised.
The paper is generally well written and honest about limitations (e.g., CFG winning in the dense regime, qualitative vs. quantitative discrepancies).
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to a single synthetic dataset (HouseExpo) at low 64×64 resolution with A*-generated, not real human, trajectories. The central motivating claim (human walking behavior) is only approximated by shortest-path planning; no real IMU/trajectory data validation weakens the practical significance claimed in the introduction.

In the dense regime, CFG outperforms CoGuide (0.97 F1 vs. 0.95, 0.95 IoU vs. 0.90), and the advantage of the proposed method narrows or disappears exactly when the problem is least ill-posed. The argument that CFG 'overfits the joint distribution' is not substantiated with evidence, and CFG may itself be an under-tuned or unfairly disadvantaged baseline.

The theoretical validity of the surrogate rests on InfoNCE achieving its optimum, which is only approximately true in practice; no analysis of the tightness of the approximation, the effect of temperature/encoder capacity on surrogate fidelity, or how far the learned embedding space deviates from the true likelihood is provided. The noise model also mismatches: DPS assumes Gaussian additive noise on A(x̂0), while trajectories are discrete A* outputs during training.

Some results appear suspicious or inconsistent: DPS+Neural A* reports identical values across all three density regimes (0.79/0.67/0.79/0.66/0.79/0.66), which is unexpected; Figure 6 labels 'DPS + DMPlug' and 'DPS + DiffPIR' inconsistently with Table 1; several typos remain ('CoGuides´', 'it's gradient', 'a proxies').

Scalability and generalization of the contrastive encoders are untested: the approach is demonstrated only on one data distribution, and out-of-distribution floorplans/trajectories, larger resolutions (the paper notes planners scale poorly), and furniture-obstacle environments are deferred to future work.

Several key components feel like empirical patches (intersection penalty, Adam-in-DDIM, LR annealing, hard-stop gating, alignment-loss scheduling) with limited principled analysis of why each is needed; the combination of tricks makes it harder to attribute gains specifically to the contrastive surrogate, though ablations partially mitigate this concern.
The claim that contrastive guidance generalizes to a broader family of non-differentiable operators is speculative — no second forward operator or application is actually demonstrated.

strengths: Novel and practical problem formulation: recovering floorplans from human-walked trajectories is a genuinely interesting instance of a non-differentiable, partially specified forward operator, largely unexplored in the diffusion-based inverse solver literature

The core idea—replacing the unstable path-planner likelihood gradient with a contrastive embedding-space surrogate—is clean, well-motivated by the Jacobian-instability analysis (Sec. 3.1, Fig. 1), and the InfoNCE-derived likelihood-to-evidence ratio (Eq. 8, Appendix A) provides a principled, if incomplete, justification for the surrogate score

Comprehensive evaluation: 6 competitive baselines (DPS variants with three differentiable planners, DiffPIR, DMPlug, CFG), three trajectory-density regimes, ablations on intersection penalty and optimizer choice, noise-robustness analysis, and uncertainty quantification

Real-world validation with UWB-collected trajectories in two apartments, demonstrating better distributional robustness than CFG, plus a bonus blind audio restoration experiment showing potential generality
Good reproducibility posture: code release promised, detailed architecture and hyperparameter documentation in Appendix C
weaknesses: Theoretical claims outrun the evidence: the surrogate-likelihood argument holds only when InfoNCE reaches its optimum with a perfect critic, and the 'smooth/Lipschitz embedding space' claim is asserted rather than proven; no formal analysis of how contrastive approximation error propagates into posterior-sampling error

The surrogate likelihood is coarse by construction: embedding-level compatibility is a much weaker constraint than pixel-level measurement consistency, and many distinct floorplans can embed near the same trajectory. The paper provides no posterior-fidelity or calibration evaluation (beyond variance of distance transforms) to verify that CoGuide samples from the true posterior rather than producing plausible-looking but biased reconstructions

The CFG baseline is very strong—best in the dense regime (Table 1) and competitive overall—since it also learns the trajectory-floorplan joint distribution; CoGuide's headline advantage is confined to the sparse regime and the qualitative real-world results, making the incremental benefit over simply training a conditional diffusion model somewhat unclear

The 'blind inverse problem' framing is partly overstated: the contrastive encoders are trained on synthetic (floorplan, trajectory) pairs generated via an approximate A* operator, so partial knowledge of A is still assumed; the audio appendix likewise trains on a known degradation family for pair generation

Limited scope of experiments: a single 64×64 synthetic dataset (HouseExPO) for the main results; no cross-dataset or resolution-generalization evaluation; real-world evaluation is qualitative only with two apartments and no quantitative metrics

Heuristic engineering components (Adam inside DDIM steps, cosine LR annealing with hard gating, intersection penalty) are introduced without theoretical grounding and could mask the actual contribution of the contrastive guidance; an ablation isolating CoGuide guidance from these tricks is only partial (Table 3, Table 2)

The audio restoration comparison lacks a strong baseline (only LTAS equalization is compared, not the full learned degradation operator method of Moliner et al. 2024), and FAD alone is a weak fidelity metric
Notational sloppiness in appendices (encoders f_phi/g_psi swapped in loss descriptions, f_psi vs g_psi inconsistency in Appendix D) slightly undermines polish

strengths: Addresses a genuinely interesting and practically motivated inverse problem (floorplan estimation from human trajectories) with a non-differentiable, partially specified forward operator, which is outside the scope of most standard diffusion-based inverse solvers.

The idea of replacing an unstable likelihood gradient with a smooth contrastive embedding-space surrogate is intuitive and clearly motivated by the instability analysis (Fig. 1) of differentiable path planners inside DPS.

Fairly broad experimental comparison: 6 baselines spanning DPS variants with different planners, DiffPIR, DMPlug, and CFG; ablations on the intersection penalty, optimizer choice, measurement noise, and trajectory density; plus real-world UWB data collection in two apartments.
The paper is generally well written, with a clear problem formulation and honest acknowledgment of limitations (e.g., CFG being strongest in the dense regime, dataset lacking furniture).
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim—that the contrastive score is a 'valid approximation' of the true likelihood score—is substantially overclaimed. The InfoNCE density-ratio argument (Eq. 8, Appendix A) holds only at the exact optimum with the specific contrastive task over data-distribution samples; learned encoders never attain this optimum, and crucially the ratio is recovered for pairs drawn from the data distribution, whereas guidance is applied to intermediate, off-manifold x̂0 states during diffusion where the learned embedding provides no density-ratio guarantee. The derivation legitimizes the heuristic but does not establish the claimed validity.

Potential circularity in the setup: all training trajectories are synthesized from floorplans via A*, so the contrastive encoders effectively learn A* itself. This undercuts the 'human path-planning is only partially known' motivation; the method reduces to learning a proxy forward model from synthetic pairs, and the gap between this proxy and real human behavior is only assessed qualitatively on two apartments.

Evaluation red flags: the DPS+Neural A* results are numerically identical across sparse/moderate/dense regimes (0.79±0.09 F1, etc.), and other DPS variants barely vary across densities, suggesting the baselines are largely insensitive to the measurement or that the evaluation protocol has issues. This deserves explanation and undermines confidence in the comparison.

The headline method (CoGuide) loses to the CFG baseline in the dense regime, and the claim that CFG's superior metrics do not 'always reflect' qualitative quality is asserted without quantitative support (e.g., no perceptual or planner-consistency metric). The best reported result (CFG+CoGuide) relies on combining with the stronger CFG prior, making the standalone contribution harder to isolate.

The method is heavily engineered: intersection penalty, Adam inside DDIM steps, cosine LR annealing with hard gating, alignment-loss scheduling, and CFG combination. These tricks likely contribute a large share of the gains, but the ablations do not cleanly disentangle the contrastive guidance from the added machinery.

Real-world evaluation is thin: only two apartments, comparison only against CFG, and no quantitative metrics; the blind-audio extension in Appendix D uses FAD against an unclear reference and a single weak baseline (LTAS), with FAD results (restored 0.84 vs. degraded 2.52) that seem implausible without a clearer evaluation protocol.

Reproducibility statement is incomplete—the code repository link is literally empty ('can be found at .'), so reproducibility cannot be verified at review time despite the extensive hyperparameter descriptions.

Broader significance is modest: the guidance idea is a plausible but incremental extension of DPS-style guidance plus standard InfoNCE, and the paper itself frames most follow-on directions (furniture, blind operators, other modalities) as future work.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem setting: inverse problems with non-differentiable, partially-specified forward operators, instantiated as floorplan reconstruction from walking trajectories. This is a genuinely interesting point on the 'operator complexity' axis of diffusion-based inverse solvers.

Clear identification and illustration of the core technical obstacle (Fig. 1): the Jacobian of the path-planning operator is large and discontinuous, making standard DPS-style likelihood guidance unstable. The analysis of why differentiable planners (NA*, TransPath, DiPPeR) still fail is convincing.

Reasonable theoretical framing: the connection between the optimal InfoNCE classifier and the likelihood-to-evidence ratio (Oord et al. 2018) is used to justify the embedding-space surrogate likelihood score, with the derivation given in the appendix and extended to the multi-positive supervised contrastive setting.

Extensive and honest evaluation: 6 baselines including DPS augmented with three differentiable planners, DiffPIR, DMPlug, and a strong CFG conditional model; three trajectory-density regimes; ablations for the intersection penalty and Adam-vs-GD guidance; measurement-noise sweeps; uncertainty quantification; and a real-world UWB data collection in two apartments that reveals distribution shift and favors CoGuide over CFG.
Demonstrated generalization beyond the spatial domain via a blind audio restoration experiment (Appendix D), supporting the broader claim about blind inverse problems.
Good reproducibility posture: open-source code commitment, public datasets, detailed architecture and hyperparameter descriptions in the appendix.
weaknesses: The theoretical 'validity' claim of the surrogate likelihood is stronger than the evidence. Eq. 8 holds only at the exact optimum of InfoNCE with effectively infinite negatives, and the extension to the supervised multi-positive objective is argued rather informally ('only a single positive is used at inference'). In practice the encoders are trained with SupCon plus an alignment loss whose effect on the recovered likelihood ratio is not analyzed, and the gradient is taken through the Tweedie estimate x̂_0, introducing approximation errors that are not characterized.

The strongest baseline (CFG) actually beats CoGuide in the dense-trajectory regime, and CoGuide's headline numbers come from CFG+CoGuide, which blurs attribution: it is unclear how much of the gain is attributable to the proposed contrastive guidance versus the conditional prior. The paper's core contribution would be better supported by a clearer decomposition and by stronger analysis of when contrastive guidance adds value over simply learning a conditional model from the same paired data.

The embedding is trained on trajectories generated by the very A* operator used to define the problem, so on synthetic data CoGuide and CFG benefit from a matched forward model; the claimed robustness advantage rests mainly on a qualitative two-apartment real-world comparison against CFG only, without quantitative metrics or additional baselines.

Single dataset (HouseExpo, downsampled to 64×64), single task family for the main results, and only one blind-audio comparison (LTAS) in the appendix. Generalization claims to 'generalized blind inverse problems' are therefore speculative.

Considerable engineering complexity in the inference procedure (Adam inside DDIM steps, cosine LR annealing, hard gating, intersection penalty, weighting schedules, several sensitive hyperparameters such as λ_int where too-large values degrade results). This suggests fragility and makes the method harder to adopt; a study of sensitivity to these knobs is thin.

The inverse-solver baselines (DiffPIR, DMPlug) perform dramatically worse than all other methods, raising the possibility of suboptimal tuning for this non-standard task, which inflates the apparent margin over 'established inverse solvers'.

Minor: the reproducibility statement contains an empty repository link ('can be found at .'), and the paper's notation occasionally switches between encoders (e.g., fφ/gψ vs. fφ/fψ in Appendix D), which hurts polish.
